As of 215 PM Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... A new Heat Advisory has been issued for 
Saturday from 11 AM until 8 PM. 

The Heat Advisory was expanded to all of central NC for today 
until 8 PM. Surface observations across the northern Piedmont up
into Virginia have shown heat indices rising into 102 to around
105 and this will likely continue until convective outflow from
developing showers/storms cool the area or until 8 PM as 
nocturnal cooling begins.

A cold front is expected to remain well to our north through 
the daylight hours on Sat. However, the hot and humid air mass 
that has plagued the southern Mid-Atlantic and Carolinas this 
week will likely be convectively contaminated by cloud debris, 
lingering outflows, and pockets of rain cooled/moistened soils 
from convection this afternoon. Additionally, A canopy of mid- 
level convective debris cloudiness from the (probably weakening)
remnants of an overnight convective cluster from OH to the 
Virginias may limit insolation and curb the heat over especially
the nrn half of cntl NC on Sat. And if that convective cluster 
were to maintain intensity more than currently forecast, which 
they oftentimes do east of the Appalachians, then a more- 
prominent cold pool/outflow and possible ongoing convection 
would further limit early day heating there. The airmass will 
nonetheless have the potential to be as hot (or nearly so) as 
previous days in the absence of those lower predictability 
influences from convection/clouds. A Heat Advisory has been 
issued for Saturday across the southern half of central NC where
confidence is greatest that at least two hours of +105 is 
probable before convection/cloud cover move into the area. This 
area may need to be adjusted with the overnight forecast update.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Scattered to locally numerous showers/storms 
will be possible through this afternoon into the evening hours.

The leading edge of a cold front is beginning to work down into
northern VA this afternoon, but is expected to stay well north 
of the forecast area. The primary triggering mechanism for 
convection is expected to be along a leading pre-frontal trough 
acting as a low-lvl convergence boundary and is draped near or 
just south of the VA/NC border. The air mass in place remains 
hot and humid with temperatures regularly in the upper 90s to 
around 100 degrees and surface dew points in the upper 60s to 
low 70s. When combined with slightly cooler 500-700mb 
temperatures on the northeast side of the lower/mid level 
subtropical ridge over the southern Appalachians and extending 
into SC, moderate to high instability is expected (1500- 3500 
MLCAPE) around the initiating boundary and locations to its 
south in central NC. Storm coverage and intensity remains 
uncertain given the lack of a strong forcing mechanism and 
minimal mid/upper lvl support from any upstream MCV's given our 
location relative to the strong ridge.

If deep convection is able to develop, mean cloud-layer winds 
of 10- 25 kts over the southern Mid-Atlantic oriented about 30 
degrees off the initiating boundary should allow for convection 
to shift off the boundary and track generally east- 
southeastward. Deep layer shear of 25-35 kts should support 
storm organization along a common cold pool within small scale 
bowing clusters, although splitting cells and transient mid-lvl 
rotation will be possible with short, straight hodographs if 
storm collisions can remain at a minimum (00z HREF highlights 
10-30% of short segments of either right or left moving storms 
in the 6-11 PM timeframe). 

Steep low-lvl lapse rates, high LCLs, and strong DCAPE, will 
favor strong diabatic cooling within collapsing deep-convection 
and result in the primary risk coming from damaging straight-
line winds, especially within any storm clusters oriented along 
a common cold pool. Isolated large hail can't be ruled out, but 
given the hot temperatures, it will likely require an incredibly
deep storm and/or some mid-lvl storm rotation to have the hail 
survive its journey to the surface. 


KEY MESSAGE 3... A conditional severe risk persists on Saturday
ahead of a cold front. 

A decaying, convectively-induced mid-level disturbance over the
lower Ohio Valley will interact with a backdoor cold front 
sliding south through the Mid-Atlantic on Saturday. Deep-layer 
shear will increase compared to Friday, with mid-level flow 
strengthening as the East Coast trough digs further west, 
supporting multicell storms capable of producing damaging wind 
gusts and large hail. A Slight Risk remains in place for the 
majority of central North Carolina. This severe threat, however,
remains conditional. Upstream decaying convection out of 
western VA could focus debris cloudiness across our northern 
tier of counties. Realistically, a gradual thinning of these 
clouds will take shape through the late morning and early 
afternoon. A southward moving effective front/outflow may then
